## In 60 seconds

A map shows what was measured. A twin is a model that can be asked "what if?". To build one, take
the map's geometry, decide which tissue is which, and tune the model until the activation it
predicts matches the activation measured at the map's points. The hard part is honesty. A model that
fits the points it was tuned on can still be wrong between them, and different parameter sets can fit
equally well. This capstone builds a small twin from a mapping case and tests it that way.

## Derivations

**Symbols used throughout.** $T(\mathbf{x})$ activation time (ms). $\mathbf{f}$ the unit fibre
direction; $v_f$ and $v_t$ the conduction velocities along and across fibres (mm/ms). $D$ the speed
tensor. $\boldsymbol\theta$ the model parameters, here one velocity per region.
$T_i^{\text{meas}}$ the activation time measured at map point $i$ and $T_i(\boldsymbol\theta)$ the
model's time there. $t_0$ an unknown timing offset (ms). $\sigma$ a monodomain conductivity.

### What a twin is

A cardiac digital twin is a model of one patient's heart whose anatomy and parameters are inferred
from that patient's data so that it reproduces the available observations [@gillette2021]. The
idea is presented as a route to diagnosis, prognosis and treatment tailored to each patient, with
early steps and open challenges reviewed in [@corral2020]. Building a twin from clinical data still
needs faster, more robust and more accurate ways of fitting anatomy and parameters [@gillette2021].
For an electroanatomic map the observations are activation times and voltages at the acquired points;
the anatomy is the map's mesh.

### A fast forward model

Fitting means running the model many times, so it must be fast. The eikonal model from m30 gives
activation times directly. Conduction speed in heart tissue depends on direction relative to the
fibres (module m09); with a speed tensor the eikonal equation becomes

$$
\sqrt{\nabla T^\top D\, \nabla T} = 1, \qquad D = v_f^2\,\mathbf{f}\mathbf{f}^\top + v_t^2\left(I - \mathbf{f}\mathbf{f}^\top\right)
$$ {#eq-m33-eikonal-aniso}

On a flat sheet with uniform fibres the solution from a point is
$T = \sqrt{(\mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{f})^2/v_f^2 + (\mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{n})^2/v_t^2}$, with
$\mathbf{n}$ perpendicular to $\mathbf{f}$: isochrones are ellipses with axis ratio $v_f/v_t$.
Eikonal-based models can be very fast: a reaction–eikonal model reproduced the extracellular
potentials, electrograms and ECGs of a full bidomain model at a computational cost more than three
orders of magnitude lower [@neic2017]. This capstone keeps the surface isotropic ($v_f = v_t$) and
fits one speed per region.

**Key takeaways**

- Twins are fitted by running a forward model many times; eikonal models make that affordable.
- Anisotropy enters through the speed tensor $D$.

### Fitting the model to the map

The map's activation times are measured against a reference signal, not against the moment the
pacing stimulus or the wave started. So model and data differ by an unknown constant offset $t_0$.
Fit it together with the parameters by least squares:

$$
J(\boldsymbol\theta, t_0) = \sum_i \left(T_i(\boldsymbol\theta) + t_0 - T_i^{\text{meas}}\right)^2,
\qquad
t_0^\ast = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i \left(T_i^{\text{meas}} - T_i(\boldsymbol\theta)\right)
$$ {#eq-m33-offset}

For any $\boldsymbol\theta$ the best offset is the mean difference, which follows from
$\partial J/\partial t_0 = 0$. Solving it in closed form leaves the optimizer only the velocities.
On a test sheet with a fast and a slow half, fitting two speeds to 60 noisy activation times with an
unknown offset recovers both speeds to within a few percent.

**Key takeaways**

- Activation times carry an unknown reference offset; solve it in closed form.
- Fit few parameters: one speed per region the data can actually inform.

### From speed to conductivity

The eikonal twin gives velocities; a reaction–diffusion simulator such as openCARP needs
conductivities [@plank2021]. In the monodomain equation, multiplying the conductivity by $k$ and
stretching all lengths by $\sqrt{k}$ leaves the equation unchanged, so the conduction velocity
scales as $\sqrt{k}$:

$$
v \propto \sqrt{\sigma} \quad\Rightarrow\quad
\sigma_{\text{new}} = \sigma_{\text{old}} \left(\frac{v_{\text{target}}}{v_{\text{sim}}}\right)^2
$$ {#eq-m33-cv-scaling}

for a fixed membrane model and surface-to-volume ratio. A test checks it on a cable: four times the
conductivity gives twice the speed, and one correction step reaches a target speed. On a discrete
mesh the relation is approximate, which is why parameterization tools iterate until the simulated
velocity matches the prescribed one [@costa2013].

**Key takeaways**

- Speed scales with the square root of conductivity; correct conductivity by the squared speed
  ratio.
- Iterate on real meshes: discretization bends the rule.

### Is the twin any good?

Error on the points used for fitting says little. Split the points into $K$ folds, fit the twin
without fold $k$, and predict fold $k$:

$$
E_{\text{CV}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{F}_k}
\left(T_i(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{-k}) + t_0^\ast - T_i^{\text{meas}}\right)^2}
$$ {#eq-m33-holdout}

where $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{-k}$ is fitted without fold $\mathcal{F}_k$. With an exact model
and no noise, $E_{\text{CV}}$ is close to zero. A model with too many parameters fits its training
points better and predicts held-out points worse; the tests show this with polynomials. For twins,
also refit from many starting points: if quite different parameter sets give the same error, the
data do not identify those parameters.

**Key takeaways**

- Judge a twin on held-out points, not on the points it was tuned to.
- Equal fits from different parameters means the data do not identify them; report the spread.
